description: Measure conversion at every stage of any funnel (sales, onboarding, hiring, user activation). The biggest drop is the biggest opportunity. Stage-by-stage conversion math reveals where value leaks out, not vanity top-of-funnel metrics.

steps.description: Define every stage from first contact to desired outcome. Each stage must be measurable and have a clear entry and exit criterion.

inputs.name: desired-outcome
inputs.desc: The end result (a sale, a hire, an active user, a habit formed)

inputs.name: current-process
inputs.desc: How people currently move from first contact to the outcome

outputs.name: funnel-stages
outputs.desc: Each stage with its entry criterion, exit criterion, and the action that moves someone from this stage to the next

outputs.name: stage-measurement-plan
outputs.desc: How to count the number of people at each stage and the time spent at each stage

process: Walk the process from the customer or user's perspective: what is the first touchpoint? What must they do to advance? What is the last step before the outcome?
Define each stage with a measurable entry criterion. 'Aware' is too vague. 'Visited the website' is measurable. 'Interested' is too vague. 'Started a free trial' is measurable.
Verify each stage has a clear action that moves someone to the next stage. If there is no clear action, the stage is not a real step.
Set up the measurement: how will you count the people at each stage? Web analytics, CRM data, manual tracking, or a combination.

steps.description: Calculate the conversion rate between every adjacent pair of stages. The rate is: number who entered the next stage divided by number who entered this stage.

inputs.name: funnel-stages
inputs.desc: The defined stages

inputs.name: stage-measurement-plan
inputs.desc: How to measure each stage

outputs.name: stage-conversion-rates
outputs.desc: The conversion rate between every adjacent stage pair, with the sample size and time period

outputs.name: biggest-drop
outputs.desc: The stage transition with the lowest conversion rate: this is the highest-leverage improvement point

process: For each stage transition, count: how many people entered the stage, and how many advanced to the next stage? The conversion rate is: advanced / entered.
Calculate for a meaningful time period (at least 30 days or 100+ people per stage to avoid small-sample noise).
Identify the biggest drop: the stage transition with the lowest conversion rate. This is where the most value leaks out of the funnel.
Also calculate the time at each stage: how long does the average person spend before advancing? Long dwell times indicate friction or confusion.

steps.description: Investigate why people drop off at the biggest-drop stage. Do not guess. Ask, observe, or test.

inputs.name: biggest-drop
inputs.desc: The stage transition with the worst conversion

inputs.name: funnel-stages
inputs.desc: The stage definitions for context

outputs.name: drop-off-reasons
outputs.desc: The specific reasons people leave at this stage, ranked by frequency

outputs.name: fix-hypotheses
outputs.desc: Testable hypotheses for improving conversion at this stage

process: Ask the dropouts: survey people who left at this stage. What stopped them? What were they expecting? What was confusing or frustrating?
Observe the behavior: watch (or track) what people do at this stage. Where do they click? Where do they hesitate? Where do they leave?
Analyze the segments: do all segments drop equally, or is the drop concentrated in one segment (mobile users, a specific source, a specific persona)?
Generate fix hypotheses: 'If we [change X], then [Y% more people] will advance because [reason Z].' Each hypothesis should be testable with an A/B test or a before/after comparison.

steps.description: Test the fix hypotheses and measure the impact. Then move to the next biggest drop. Continuous improvement, one stage at a time.

inputs.name: fix-hypotheses
inputs.desc: The testable hypotheses

inputs.name: stage-conversion-rates
inputs.desc: The baseline conversion rates

outputs.name: test-results
outputs.desc: The results of each fix: the change in conversion rate at the target stage and the change in overall funnel throughput

outputs.name: updated-funnel-metrics
outputs.desc: The new conversion rates after the fix, with the next biggest drop identified for the next cycle

process: Test the top hypothesis. Use an A/B test if you have enough traffic. Use a before/after comparison if you do not.
Measure the impact at the target stage AND on overall funnel throughput. A fix that improves one stage but worsens the next is not a net improvement.
If the fix works, implement it permanently. Update the baseline conversion rates.
Identify the next biggest drop. Repeat the cycle. Over time, the funnel tightens and overall throughput increases.

description: Plot retention over time. If the curve flattens, you have a product or service that retains. If it trends to zero, you have a leaky bucket. Fixing retention is higher leverage than increasing acquisition because retained users compound while acquired users leak.

steps.description: Plot the retention curve: percentage of users or customers remaining at each time period after their start date.

inputs.name: user-data
inputs.desc: User activity data with start dates and activity timestamps

inputs.name: retention-definition
inputs.desc: What counts as retained (logged in, purchased, attended, continued a habit)

outputs.name: retention-curve
outputs.desc: The curve: percentage retained at each time period (day 1, day 7, day 30, day 90, day 180, day 365)

outputs.name: curve-shape
outputs.desc: The shape classification: flattening (good), declining to zero (leaky bucket), or improving over time (ideal)

process: Define retention: what action indicates the person is still active? Log in, make a purchase, attend, exercise, use the feature.
For each time period, calculate the percentage of the starting cohort that is still retained.
Plot the curve. Look at the shape, not just the final number.
Classify: does it flatten (a stable base of retained users), decline to zero (everyone eventually leaves), or improve (users who stay get more engaged over time)?

steps.description: Find the critical period: the time window where most drop-off occurs. This is the intervention point.

inputs.name: retention-curve
inputs.desc: The plotted retention curve

inputs.name: curve-shape
inputs.desc: The shape classification

outputs.name: critical-period
outputs.desc: The time window with the steepest drop-off (e.g., days 3-7 or month 1-2)

outputs.name: retention-benchmarks
outputs.desc: The retention rate at key time points (day 1, day 7, day 30) compared to industry benchmarks if available

process: Calculate the period-over-period drop-off rate. Which period loses the highest percentage of remaining users?
The critical period is where the curve drops fastest. If 40% leave in the first week but only 5% per month after that, the first week is the critical period.
Compare to benchmarks: for SaaS, day-1 retention above 80% and day-30 above 40% is typical. For consumer apps, day-1 above 40% and day-30 above 15% is typical.
The critical period tells you where to focus. Improving retention in the first week is higher leverage than improving it in month 6.

steps.description: Design interventions targeted at the critical period. The intervention must address why people leave, not just remind them to stay.

inputs.name: critical-period
inputs.desc: The time window to target

inputs.name: retention-curve
inputs.desc: The retention data for context

outputs.name: intervention-plan
outputs.desc: Specific interventions during the critical period: what to deliver, when, and through what channel

outputs.name: success-criteria
outputs.desc: How to measure whether the intervention improved retention: the target retention rate at the end of the critical period

process: Investigate why people leave during the critical period: survey, behavioral analysis, or user interviews.

Design the intervention to address the reason, not just the symptom. If people leave because they did not find value, show them the value faster. If they leave because of friction, remove the friction. If they leave because of confusion, clarify.
Time the intervention: deliver it before the drop-off peak, not after. If the biggest drop is on day 5, the intervention must arrive by day 3.
Measure the impact: compare the retention curve before and after the intervention. Or run an A/B test with intervention vs. no intervention.

description: Determine the optimal price range using the Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter. Ask four price questions, plot the curves, find the acceptable range and the optimal price point. Better than guessing. Works for products, services, subscriptions, and fees.

steps.description: Build and administer the Van Westendorp survey: four questions about price perception.

inputs.name: product-description
inputs.desc: What is being priced, described clearly enough for the respondent to assess value

inputs.name: target-audience
inputs.desc: Who will answer the survey (current customers, prospects, market segment)

outputs.name: survey-instrument
outputs.desc: The four Van Westendorp questions, customized for the product, with the response format (open-ended price entry)

outputs.name: survey-data
outputs.desc: The raw responses: for each respondent, four price points (too cheap, cheap, expensive, too expensive)

process: Ask four questions about the same product: 1) At what price would you consider this product so inexpensive that you would question its quality? (too cheap) 2) At what price would you consider this product a bargain, a great buy for the money? (cheap) 3) At what price would this product begin to seem expensive, although you might still consider buying it? (expensive) 4) At what price would this product be too expensive to consider? (too expensive)
Each question requires an open-ended price response. Do not use ranges or multiple choice.
Administer to at least 100 respondents from the target audience. More respondents produce smoother curves.
Collect demographic data alongside the price data to segment the analysis later.

steps.description: Plot the four cumulative frequency curves and find the intersection points that define the acceptable price range.

inputs.name: survey-data
inputs.desc: The raw price perception data from respondents

outputs.name: price-curves
outputs.desc: The four cumulative frequency curves: too cheap (cumulative descending), cheap (cumulative descending), expensive (cumulative ascending), too expensive (cumulative ascending)

outputs.name: intersection-points
outputs.desc: The key intersections: Point of Marginal Cheapness (too cheap meets expensive), Optimal Price Point (too cheap meets too expensive), Indifference Price Point (cheap meets expensive), Point of Marginal Expensiveness (cheap meets too expensive)

process: For each of the four questions, create a cumulative frequency distribution: for 'too cheap' and 'cheap,' plot cumulative percentage descending (what % said this price or higher). For 'expensive' and 'too expensive,' plot cumulative percentage ascending (what % said this price or lower).
Find the intersections: the Optimal Price Point is where the 'too cheap' and 'too expensive' curves cross. The Indifference Price Point is where the 'cheap' and 'expensive' curves cross.
The acceptable price range is between the Point of Marginal Cheapness (too cheap meets expensive) and the Point of Marginal Expensiveness (cheap meets too expensive).
The optimal price is within this range, near the Indifference Price Point. Pricing below the range signals low quality. Pricing above the range loses customers.

steps.description: Use the Van Westendorp results to make the pricing decision. Combine with cost data and competitive positioning.

inputs.name: intersection-points
inputs.desc: The price range and optimal point from the analysis

inputs.name: product-description
inputs.desc: The product context, costs, and competitive landscape

outputs.name: pricing-recommendation
outputs.desc: The recommended price with the range it falls within and the reasoning: Van Westendorp range, cost floor, competitive position

outputs.name: price-test-plan
outputs.desc: If uncertain: a plan to A/B test 2-3 prices within the acceptable range to find the revenue-maximizing point

process: Set the floor: the price must cover costs plus the target margin. If the Van Westendorp range is entirely below the cost floor, the product cannot be sold profitably at market-acceptable prices.
Set the ceiling: the Point of Marginal Expensiveness. Above this, customer acquisition drops sharply.
Position within the range: near the top for premium positioning, near the middle for market rate, near the bottom for volume or penetration.
If the range is wide, consider testing 2-3 prices: the Van Westendorp optimal point, a price 10% above, and a price 10% below. Measure which produces the highest revenue (price times quantity).

description: Diagnose churn by behavior, not by exit surveys. Exit surveys lie because people rationalize after the fact. Behavior before churn tells the truth. Identify the behavioral signals that predict churn 30-60 days in advance, then intervene before it happens.

steps.description: Compare the behavior of people who churned vs. people who stayed. The differences reveal the predictive signals.

inputs.name: user-activity-data
inputs.desc: Activity data for churned and retained users over the 90 days before churn

inputs.name: churn-definition
inputs.desc: How churn is defined (cancelled subscription, no login in 30 days, no purchase in 90 days)

outputs.name: behavioral-differences
outputs.desc: The behaviors that are statistically different between churners and retainers: login frequency, feature usage, support tickets, engagement patterns

outputs.name: candidate-churn-signals
outputs.desc: The 3-5 behaviors most predictive of future churn, ranked by signal strength

process: Pull activity data for two groups: people who churned in the last 6 months and a matched sample of people who did not churn during the same period.

Compare their behavior in the 90 days before the churn event (or the equivalent period for the retained group): login frequency, feature usage breadth, engagement depth, support ticket volume, billing issues, response to communications.
Find the statistically significant differences: which behaviors are different enough that the difference is unlikely to be random?
Rank the differences by signal strength: which behavior change most reliably precedes churn?

steps.description: Validate the candidate churn signals on a holdout sample. A signal that works on the training data but not on new data is overfitted.

inputs.name: candidate-churn-signals
inputs.desc: The candidate predictive signals

inputs.name: user-activity-data
inputs.desc: A separate holdout dataset for validation

outputs.name: validated-signals
outputs.desc: The signals that predict churn on the holdout data, with their lead time (how far before churn the signal appears) and accuracy

outputs.name: churn-risk-scorecard
outputs.desc: A scoring system: users with [signal A + signal B] have [X%] probability of churning within [Y days]

process: Apply the candidate signals to the holdout data: do they correctly identify the users who later churned?
Measure the lead time: how many days before churn does each signal appear? A signal that appears 3 days before churn leaves no time to intervene. A signal at 60 days gives plenty of time.
Measure accuracy: what percentage of flagged users actually churned (precision)? What percentage of actual churners were flagged (recall)?
Build the scorecard: combine the validated signals into a risk score. Users with multiple signals are highest risk.

steps.description: Design interventions for users who show churn signals. The intervention must address the behavior change, not just remind the user to stay.

inputs.name: validated-signals
inputs.desc: The predictive churn signals

inputs.name: churn-risk-scorecard
inputs.desc: The risk scoring system

outputs.name: intervention-playbook
outputs.desc: For each risk level: the intervention (personal outreach, feature education, special offer, product fix), the timing, and the channel

outputs.name: intervention-effectiveness-plan
outputs.desc: How to measure whether the intervention reduces churn: compare intervention group vs. control group

process: For high-risk users: personal outreach (a call or personal email) to understand what changed and whether you can help. This is the highest-touch, highest-impact intervention.

For medium-risk users: targeted communication based on the specific signal. If usage dropped, send a use-case guide. If a support ticket went unresolved, escalate it. If engagement shifted to fewer features, show related features.
For low-risk users: automated engagement (tips, case studies, new features) to maintain the relationship without personal touch.
Measure effectiveness: split the at-risk users into intervention and control groups. Compare their churn rates over 90 days. If the intervention group churns less, the intervention is working.

description: Design the activation sequence: the steps between sign-up and first value. This is where most users die. Map the milestones, measure drop-off at each, and remove friction from the highest-drop step. A user who reaches the activation milestone is 3-5x more likely to retain.

steps.description: Define the activation milestone: the specific action that indicates the user has experienced the core value.

inputs.name: product-or-service
inputs.desc: What the user signed up for

inputs.name: core-value
inputs.desc: The primary value the user expects to receive

outputs.name: activation-milestone
outputs.desc: The single measurable action that best indicates the user experienced core value (e.g., sent their first message, completed their first workout, made their first sale)

outputs.name: activation-steps
outputs.desc: Every step between sign-up and the activation milestone, with the required action at each step

process: Define the core value: what is the one thing the user came for? For a communication tool: sending and receiving messages. For a fitness app: completing a workout. For a marketplace: making a sale.
Define the activation milestone: the first time the user experiences that core value. It must be a measurable, specific action.
Map every step between sign-up and the milestone: account creation, profile setup, onboarding flow, first feature interaction, and the milestone itself.
Each step must be necessary. If a step is not needed to reach the milestone, remove it from the path.

steps.description: Measure drop-off at each step between sign-up and activation.

inputs.name: activation-steps
inputs.desc: The steps in the activation path

inputs.name: activation-milestone
inputs.desc: The target milestone

outputs.name: step-conversion-rates
outputs.desc: The percentage of users who complete each step, sequentially

outputs.name: highest-drop-step
outputs.desc: The step with the worst conversion rate: this is the activation bottleneck

process: For each step, count: how many users reached this step, and how many advanced to the next? Calculate the conversion rate.
Also measure: how long does each step take? Steps that take too long have friction even if the conversion rate looks acceptable.
Identify the highest-drop step: where do you lose the most users? This is the bottleneck.
Calculate the overall activation rate: percentage of sign-ups who reach the activation milestone. This is the headline metric for the activation sequence.

steps.description: Remove friction from the highest-drop step. Then move to the next.

inputs.name: highest-drop-step
inputs.desc: The activation bottleneck

inputs.name: step-conversion-rates
inputs.desc: The baseline rates

outputs.name: friction-diagnosis
outputs.desc: Why users drop at this step: confusion, too many required fields, unclear instructions, missing context, technical error

outputs.name: friction-fix-plan
outputs.desc: Specific changes to reduce friction: simplify, remove optional steps, add guidance, fix errors, reduce time required

process: Diagnose the friction: observe users attempting the step (screen recordings, user testing), survey users who dropped, and analyze the interaction data (time on step, error rates, back-button clicks).

Categorize the friction: complexity (too many choices or steps), confusion (unclear what to do), effort (requires too much input), technical (errors or slow loading), or motivation (user does not see why this step is needed).
Fix the dominant friction type: simplify choices, clarify instructions, reduce required input, fix technical issues, or show the user why this step leads to value.
Measure the impact: A/B test or before/after. Improve the step, measure the new conversion rate, and calculate the impact on overall activation rate.

description: Calculate the viral coefficient (K-factor): invitations per user times the conversion rate of those invitations. K greater than 1 means organic growth exceeds churn. K less than 1 means you need paid acquisition indefinitely. Design for referral, measure the coefficient, optimize the loop.

steps.description: Map the referral loop: how does a user invite another user, and what is the experience of the invited user?

inputs.name: product-or-service
inputs.desc: What the user is referring

inputs.name: current-referral-mechanism
inputs.desc: How users currently refer others (if any)

outputs.name: referral-loop-map
outputs.desc: The step-by-step loop: user action to invite, invitation delivery, invited user's experience, conversion of invited user, new user's action to invite

outputs.name: loop-friction-points
outputs.desc: Where the loop is difficult, slow, or unclear

process: Map each step: what does the existing user do to invite? (Share a link, send an email, tell someone, use an in-product invite feature.) How is the invitation delivered? What does the invited person see? What must they do to convert?
Identify the friction points: is the invite action easy to find? Is the invitation compelling? Is the conversion process simple?
If there is no referral mechanism, design one. The simplest: a shareable link with a clear benefit for both the referrer and the invitee.
Map the loop back to the beginning: once the new user is onboarded, how likely are they to invite someone? This closes the loop.

steps.description: Calculate the K-factor: invitations per user times the invitation conversion rate.

inputs.name: referral-loop-map
inputs.desc: The referral loop structure

inputs.name: referral-data
inputs.desc: Data on invitations sent and converted (if available)

outputs.name: k-factor
outputs.desc: The viral coefficient: K = (invitations per user) x (conversion rate per invitation). K > 1 means viral growth.

outputs.name: k-factor-components
outputs.desc: The two components: invitation rate (what percentage of users invite, and how many invitations each) and conversion rate (what percentage of invited people become users)

process: Measure the invitation rate: what percentage of users send at least one invitation? Of those, how many invitations do they send on average?
Measure the conversion rate: of all invitations sent, what percentage result in a new user?
Calculate K: invitations per user (total invitations / total users) times conversion rate.

If K > 1: viral growth. Each user generates more than one new user. If K < 1: you need paid acquisition to grow. If K = 0.5: each user generates half a new user, which helps but does not sustain growth alone.

steps.description: Optimize the K-factor by increasing invitation rate or invitation conversion rate. Small improvements in either component multiply through the loop.

inputs.name: k-factor-components
inputs.desc: The invitation rate and conversion rate

inputs.name: loop-friction-points
inputs.desc: The friction in the referral loop

outputs.name: optimization-plan
outputs.desc: Specific changes to improve each component: make inviting easier (rate), make the invitation more compelling (conversion), reduce friction in the invited user's conversion path

outputs.name: projected-k-factor
outputs.desc: The expected K-factor after optimizations, with the assumptions behind the projection

process: To increase invitation rate: make the invite action visible and easy. Trigger it at moments of delight (after the user experiences value). Reward the referrer (discount, credit, recognition).

To increase conversion rate: make the invitation personal (from a named person, not the company). Show the invitee what they will gain. Reduce the steps to convert (pre-filled forms, single-click sign-up).
Test each optimization independently. Measure the impact on the specific component and on the overall K-factor.
Small improvements compound: increasing invitation rate from 0.5 to 0.7 and conversion from 0.3 to 0.4 moves K from 0.15 to 0.28, nearly doubling organic growth contribution.

description: Determine which acquisition channels produce the highest quality at the lowest cost. Cost per acquisition by channel, adjusted for lifetime value. Most channels look good on volume and bad on value. The channel that produces the most sign-ups is not necessarily the best channel.

steps.description: Calculate the true cost per acquisition for each channel, including all costs (not just ad spend).

inputs.name: acquisition-channels
inputs.desc: All channels used to acquire users or customers (paid ads, organic search, referral, social, content, events, partnerships)

inputs.name: channel-spend
inputs.desc: The total spend per channel including ad costs, content creation, tooling, and time

outputs.name: cost-per-acquisition-by-channel
outputs.desc: The fully loaded cost to acquire one user or customer through each channel

outputs.name: channel-volume
outputs.desc: The number of acquisitions through each channel per period

process: For each channel, sum ALL costs: ad spend, content creation time (valued at hourly rate), tool costs, agency fees, event costs, and staff time spent managing the channel.
Divide by the number of acquisitions attributed to the channel. This is the fully loaded cost per acquisition.
Do not use the channel's self-reported numbers (ad platform attribution). Use your own tracking. Ad platforms over-attribute because they take credit for conversions that would have happened anyway.
Rank channels by cost per acquisition. But do not stop here: the cheapest channel may produce the lowest-value customers.

steps.description: Measure the quality of users from each channel: do they activate, retain, and generate revenue, or do they sign up and leave?

inputs.name: cost-per-acquisition-by-channel
inputs.desc: The cost data by channel

inputs.name: acquisition-channels
inputs.desc: The channels to analyze

outputs.name: channel-quality-metrics
outputs.desc: For each channel: activation rate, 30-day retention, 90-day retention, and average revenue per user

outputs.name: channel-ltv-estimate
outputs.desc: The estimated lifetime value of users from each channel

process: For users from each channel, calculate: what percentage activated (reached the activation milestone)? What percentage retained at 30 and 90 days? What is the average revenue per user?
Estimate the lifetime value (LTV) for each channel's users: retained revenue over the expected lifetime.
Compare the LTV to the cost per acquisition. A channel with $50 CPA and $500 LTV is more valuable than a channel with $10 CPA and $30 LTV.
Rank channels by LTV:CPA ratio. This is the true measure of channel quality, not the volume or the cost alone.

steps.description: Optimize channel investment based on quality-adjusted cost. Shift spend from low-LTV channels to high-LTV channels.

inputs.name: channel-quality-metrics
inputs.desc: The quality data by channel

inputs.name: channel-ltv-estimate
inputs.desc: The LTV estimates by channel

outputs.name: channel-investment-plan
outputs.desc: For each channel: increase, maintain, decrease, or stop, with the reallocation amounts and the expected impact on overall acquisition quality

outputs.name: channel-monitoring-dashboard
outputs.desc: The metrics to track monthly: CPA, activation rate, retention, LTV:CPA ratio by channel

process: Increase investment in channels with the highest LTV:CPA ratio, up to the point of diminishing returns (the CPA starts rising as you exhaust the audience).
Decrease investment in channels with low LTV:CPA ratio. If the ratio is below 1 (you spend more to acquire than the customer generates), the channel destroys value.
Test new channels with a small budget. Measure the LTV:CPA ratio before scaling.
Monitor monthly: as you increase spend on a channel, does the LTV:CPA ratio hold or decline? Declining ratio means you are reaching diminishing returns for that channel.

description: Determine whether your product or community has a network effect (each new user makes it more valuable for existing users). If yes, build the effect deliberately. If no, you are in a linear business. Design for density in a small market before breadth in a large one.

steps.description: Determine if a network effect exists and what type it is.

inputs.name: product-description
inputs.desc: What the product or service does

inputs.name: user-interaction-model
inputs.desc: How users interact with each other or with the product's content

outputs.name: network-effect-type
outputs.desc: The type of network effect: direct (users interact with each other, e.g., phone network), indirect (users benefit from complementary supply, e.g., marketplace), data (more usage improves the product, e.g., recommendation engine), or none

outputs.name: effect-strength-assessment
outputs.desc: How strong the effect is: does adding 10% more users create a noticeable improvement for existing users?

process: Ask: does the product become more valuable as more people use it? If adding 100 users makes the product better for the existing 1000, there is a network effect. If not, the value is independent of the user count.

Classify the type: direct (users communicate or transact with each other), indirect (more buyers attract more sellers and vice versa), or data (more usage data improves recommendations, search results, or predictions).

Assess the strength: is the effect strong enough that users notice? A marketplace with 10 sellers vs. 100 sellers has a strong effect. A tool where users work independently has a weak or absent effect.
If there is no network effect, growth must be driven by product quality and marketing, not by the user base itself. This is not bad. It just means the growth model is different.

steps.description: Build density in a small market before expanding broadly. Network effects are strongest in concentrated networks and weakest in sparse ones.

inputs.name: network-effect-type
inputs.desc: The type and strength of the network effect

inputs.name: product-description
inputs.desc: The product context

outputs.name: target-market-selection
outputs.desc: The initial market to dominate: small enough to achieve density quickly, valuable enough to sustain the business

outputs.name: density-strategy
outputs.desc: How to achieve density: geographic focus, niche focus, community focus, or use-case focus

process: Select the smallest market where density creates a self-sustaining loop. For a marketplace: a single city or category. For a social product: a single community or organization. For a data product: a single use case.

Define density: what user or supply count makes the product clearly valuable in this market? For a marketplace, it might be 50 active sellers in one category. For a social product, it might be 200 active users in one community.
Focus all acquisition efforts on reaching density in this market before expanding. Spreading across multiple markets creates sparse networks where no user sees enough value.
The sign that density is achieved: organic growth in the target market (users invite users without paid acquisition) and retention is stable.

steps.description: Measure the network effect: as the user base grows, does engagement, retention, or value per user increase?

inputs.name: density-strategy
inputs.desc: The density approach being executed

inputs.name: network-effect-type
inputs.desc: The effect type for measurement design

outputs.name: network-effect-metrics
outputs.desc: Metrics that track the network effect: engagement per user vs. total users, retention vs. network size, value per transaction vs. supply count

outputs.name: effect-curve
outputs.desc: The curve showing how user value changes with network size: linear (no effect), convex (strong effect), or concave (diminishing effect)

process: Track the proxy metric for the network effect type. For direct: interactions per user as user count grows. For indirect: matches per participant as supply and demand grow. For data: prediction accuracy or recommendation relevance as data volume grows.

Plot the curve: does the metric increase as the network grows? If yes, the network effect is working. If it flatlines, the effect may be weak or the product may not facilitate the connection between users well enough.
Compare across markets: is the network effect stronger in your dense market vs. sparse markets? This validates the density strategy.
Watch for negative network effects: if the product becomes worse as it grows (spam, noise, congestion), you have a scaling problem that will cap growth.
